newsitem.title: UK: Coffee rally is extended, consumers pay.
newsitem.headline: Coffee rally is extended, consumers pay.

text.p: Buying by speculative funds reignited a rally in world coffee prices on Monday and a big European roaster, Douwe Egberts of the Netherlands, said it was now having to pass on the cost to consumers at the supermarket check-out.
An explosive rally has taken the price of coffee beans in the futures pits up by about 25 percent since the end of 1996. Traders cite low stocks and and doubts about the size of Brazil's crop.
According to brokerage GNI Ltd "there is potential for a very sharp price spike should supply disruptions occur".
Action was brisk on Monday in New York futures for the Arabica type of coffee despite data that showed a rise in speculative long positions.

The New York March contract soon traded more than 5-1/2 cents higher at 145.40 cents a lb. London Robusta later futures ended at $1,530 per tonne, up $30 on the day and compared with $1,235 on the last trading day of 1996.
Recent factors to support the price have included an accord last month on new export curbs by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries and prospects of a lower-than-expected Brazil crop.
Indonesia said on Monday it would cut first half 1997 coffee exports by 150,000 60-kg bags as part of the producer bid to lock in firmer prices.
The retail price rise by Douwe Egberts is the most significant in Europe so far.

A spokesman for Douwe Egberts, with 70 percent of the Dutch market, said its retail price rise, which works out at about seven percent on the average for a 250-gramme pack, was a response to higher world prices.
"We have made the decision because of the higher structural price of coffee on the world market and because of the effects of the dollar," spokesman Joost den Haan said.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, the outlook for wheat prices was again weaker which may offset the impact of higher beverage costs.
Big purchases by Egypt of 500,000 tonnes of French wheat were said by traders to have been cheap - at $140.50 to $143.90 per tonne - but not out of line with present trends.

Bellwether Chicago wheat futures sank to $3.57 per bushel for the March position on Friday, a contract low, but were somewhat recovered on Monday to around $3.60. Cargill Inc bought one million bushels, the traders said.
But Chicago futures are now down by 50 percent from a "spike" to which they were driven a year ago after drought in Russia, Australia and North African created a tight world grain market.

The price of gold steadied on Monday after it had dropped to new 3-1/4 year lows on Friday. It was fixed in the London afternoon at $344.30 an ounce. Crude oil was somewhat easier after a late sell-off Friday.
